title: Check yourself: thread safety of common data structures

blocks.text: Questions on what this page has just taught. Choose one answer for each.

questions.stem: A cache warm-up splits 40,000 product ids among 8 threads. Each thread puts its own ids into one shared HashMap, and no id appears in two threads' shares. What can the map look like once the threads are done?

options.text: It holds all 40,000 entries, since different keys land in different buckets and no two threads write into one bucket
options.says: different keys still share the map's table, and a put during another thread's resize or linking loses entries

options.text: It holds all 40,000 entries, since put() links each new entry into the table before the next put() can begin
options.says: the puts of different threads run inside a plain HashMap at the same time, which is how their resizes and links overwrite each other

options.text: It may hold fewer, since threads that link entries or resize the table at the same time overwrite each other's work
options.says: the table is shared whatever the keys; concurrent puts lose entries, and can also throw or never return

options.text: It may hold fewer, since two keys that land in one bucket make the second put() replace the first key's entry
options.says: one thread alone keeps every distinct key, colliding or not; the entries are lost because threads change the shared table at the same time

origin.section: A Plain HashMap Shared by Writers Loses Entries and Can Hang

questions.stem: Fifty threads reserve stock with `int left = stock.get(sku); if (left > 0) stock.put(sku, left - 1);` on `Collections.synchronizedMap(new HashMap<>())`, and the shop oversells. Which change stops the overselling?

options.text: Switching the map to a ConcurrentHashMap, since its lock on the key's bin lasts from the get() to the put() that follows
options.says: each call is atomic on its own; nothing is held between the get and the put, on either map

options.text: Switching the map to a ConcurrentHashMap, since its get() reads without a lock and so sees each put() at once
options.says: seeing the latest value doesn't help: two threads can still read the same value before either writes

options.text: Moving the two calls into one compute() on the map, since the map runs that read and write as one step
options.says: compute and merge read and write in one atomic call, on the wrapper and on ConcurrentHashMap alike

options.text: Moving the two calls into a block synchronized on the HashMap inside the wrapper, since that map is what the wrapper's calls lock
options.says: the wrapper's lock is the wrapper object itself, so a block on the inner HashMap excludes no other caller

origin.section: A Synchronized Wrapper Makes Each Call Atomic, Not a Sequence of Calls

questions.stem: Scanner threads record serial numbers per warehouse with `serials.computeIfAbsent(warehouse, w -> new ArrayList<>()).add(serial)`, where serials is a ConcurrentHashMap. What happens when many scanners in one warehouse scan at once?

options.text: Serials can go missing, since add() runs on one ArrayList from many threads after computeIfAbsent() has returned
options.says: the map's atomicity covers finding or creating the list; the list itself is a plain ArrayList shared by every scanner

options.text: Serials can go missing, since computeIfAbsent() can create two lists for one warehouse and keep only the second
options.says: computeIfAbsent runs the factory at most once per missing key and returns the same list to every caller

options.text: Every serial is kept, since computeIfAbsent() keeps the warehouse's entry locked until add() has finished
options.says: the call returns before add() runs; nothing the map does covers the add

options.text: Every serial is kept, since a value stored in a ConcurrentHashMap is safe to change from any thread
options.says: the map guards its entries, not the objects stored in them; a shared value needs its own thread safety

origin.section: A Thread-Safe Map Guards Its Entries, Not the Objects Stored in Them

questions.stem: A gateway keeps about 300 routes in a list that every request reads and that changes only on deploy. It also keeps an audit trail that gets one entry per request, 20,000 a second, and is read once an hour. Which pair of lists suits them?

options.text: Routes in a CopyOnWriteArrayList and the trail in a synchronized list, since a copy per write costs little when writes are rare
options.says: a copy per write is cheap for rare deploys and readers never wait; the trail would copy a growing array on every request

options.text: Routes in a CopyOnWriteArrayList and the trail in one too, since a walk over either list never waits for a writer
options.says: every add copies the whole array, so a trail growing 20,000 times a second gets slower with every entry

options.text: Routes in a synchronized list and the trail in a CopyOnWriteArrayList, since a copy per write keeps each append short
options.says: each write copies the whole array, which makes appends the expensive operation

options.text: Routes in a synchronized list and the trail in one too, since a reader of a CopyOnWriteArrayList waits while a write copies it
options.says: reads and walks use whichever array is current and never wait for a write

origin.section: CopyOnWriteArrayList Copies the Whole Array on Every Write

concepts: CopyOnWriteArrayList copies the whole array on every write, so it suits lists read far more often than written; its walks never wait for a writer and never throw.
A plain HashMap written by several threads loses entries even when no key is written twice, and can throw or never return from put(), because the threads share its table.
computeIfAbsent followed by add on a plain ArrayList value loses elements and can throw, because the add runs after the map's atomic call.
